deep.reconstruction:
This page is the continuation of Gauss's scientific diary (Tagebuch), entries of January–February 1797, numbered 51–58 in Klein's edition. Each line is a dated claim, not a worked derivation. The steps I add below are mine.

(51) Jan 8, 1797: 'Curvam lemniscatam a ∫dx/√(1−x⁴) pendentem perscrutari coepi.' 'elasticam' is struck out and replaced by 'lemniscatam'. He has begun to investigate the lemniscate, whose arc length is s(x)=∫_0^x dt/√(1−t⁴). This follows the previous page (Jan 7), where integrals such as ∫√(sin x)dx and ∫dx/√(sin x) were reduced to ∫dy/√(1−y⁴) via y²=tan x and similar substitutions. This is the start of his theory of lemniscatic functions: the inversion x=sl(s) and the period ϖ=2∫_0^1 dt/√(1−t⁴).

(52) Jan 10: 'Criterii Euleriani rationem sponte detexi.' He found for himself the reason behind Euler's criterion. For an odd prime p and p∤a: a^((p−1)/2) ≡ 1 (mod p) if a is a quadratic residue, and ≡ −1 otherwise.
- Implicit argument (mine): the units mod p form a cyclic group, and a is a residue iff a is an even power of a primitive root g.
- g^((p−1)/2) ≡ −1, because it squares to 1 and is not 1.
- This proof appears in Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (DA) §106.

(53) Jan 12: 'Integrale complet. ∫dx/ⁿ√(1−xⁿ) ad circ. quadr. reducere commentus sum.' The complete integral reduces to the quadrature of the circle, i.e. it is a rational multiple of π divided by a sine.
- Reconstruction (mine): put t=xⁿ.
- Then ∫_0^1 (1−xⁿ)^(−1/n) dx = (1/n)B(1/n, 1−1/n) = (1/n)Γ(1/n)Γ(1−1/n) = π/(n·sin(π/n)).

(54) Same date: 'Methodus facilis ∫x^(n−1)dx/(1+x^m) determinandi.' An easy method for this integral. Presumably the complete integral over (0,∞) is meant:
- ∫_0^∞ x^(n−1)/(1+x^m) dx = π/(m·sin(nπ/m)) for 0<n<m.
- It can be obtained by partial fractions over the m-th roots of −1, or by t=x^m and the reflection formula.
- With x^n=t/(1−t)-type substitutions it is equivalent to (53).

(55) Göttingen, Jan 19: 'Supplementum eximium ad polygonorum descriptionem.' Let p be prime and p−1 = a·b·c·d… (prime factors). To describe the p-gon one needs nothing else than:
- 1° division of an arbitrary arc into a, b, c, d… equal parts;
- 2° description of the a-, b-, c-, d…-gons.
In modern terms, the cyclotomic equation is solved by a chain of Gaussian periods. Each step is a cyclic equation of prime degree q (q a factor of p−1). By Lagrange resolvents, such a step reduces to extracting a q-th root, i.e. dividing an angle into q parts, plus knowing the q-th roots of unity, i.e. the q-gon. This generalises the 2^k case (the 17-gon) to arbitrary p. It is the content of DA §§359–360, the solvability of cyclotomic equations by radicals.

(56) Göttingen, Feb 4: 'Theoremata de residuis −1, ∓2 simili methodo demonstrata ut cetera.' The supplementary laws of quadratic reciprocity are proved by the same method as the other cases:
- −1 is a residue of p iff p≡1 (mod 4);
- 2 is a residue iff p≡±1 (mod 8);
- −2 is a residue iff p≡1,3 (mod 8).

(57) Feb 6: 'Forma aa+bb+cc−bc−ac−ab quoad divisores attinet convenit cum hac aa+3bb.' Implicit steps (mine):
- a²+b²+c²−ab−bc−ca = ½[(a−b)²+(b−c)²+(c−a)²].
- With x=a−c, y=b−c this becomes x²−xy+y².
- 4(x²−xy+y²) = (2x−y)²+3y².
- Hence the odd prime divisors of (primitive) values are 3 and the primes ≡1 (mod 3), exactly as for a²+3b².
- The ternary form is also the cofactor in a³+b³+c³−3abc = (a+b+c)(a²+b²+c²−ab−bc−ca).

(58) Feb 16: 'Amplificatio prop. penult. p. 1.' This generalises the penultimate proposition of diary page 1 (entry 7, a continued fraction for 1−2+8−64+…). The claim is
1 − a + a³ − a⁶ + a¹⁰ − … = Σ_{k≥0} (−1)^k a^(k(k+1)/2) = 1/(1+ a/(1+ (a²−a)/(1+ a³/(1+ (a⁴−a²)/(1+ a⁵/(1+ …)))))).
- Partial numerators: c_{2k−1} = a^(2k−1) and c_{2k} = a^(2k) − a^k = −a^k(1−a^k).
- I checked by bottom-up expansion that the truncated fraction agrees with 1−a+a³−a⁶ through a⁶. The truncation was 1/(1+a/(1+(a²−a)/(1+a³/(1+(a⁴−a²)/(1+a⁵))))), with the denominator built up as 1+a+a²−a⁴−2a⁵−a⁶+O(a⁷).
- Marginal note: 'Unde facile omnes series ubi exponentes seriem secundi ordinis constituunt transformantur.' From this, all series whose exponents form an arithmetic progression of second order (quadratic exponents, i.e. theta-type series) are easily transformed.
errors: No mathematical errors are visible. The page records results, not computations.

Entry 57 is only correct for odd divisors. Primitive values of x²−xy+y² are never even, while x²+3y² with x and y both odd is divisible by 4. So 'convenit quoad divisores' must be read as concerning odd prime divisors.
Entry 54 does not state its limits. The closed form π/(m·sin(nπ/m)) needs the range 0..∞ and 0<n<m.

results.what: Beginning of the study of the lemniscate integral ∫dx/√(1−x⁴) (diary entry 51)
results.modern_name: Lemniscatic elliptic functions; inversion of the lemniscatic integral
results.usually_credited_to: Fagnano and Euler for the integral (addition theorems); Gauss for the lemniscatic functions (1797, unpublished); Abel and Jacobi published in 1827–29
Euler (1761); the proof via primitive roots is in Gauss, DA §106

results.modern_name: Beta integral B(1/n, 1−1/n) / Euler reflection formula

results.what: Constructing the p-gon reduces to angle division into q parts and constructing q-gons for the prime factors q of p−1 (entry 55)
results.modern_name: Solvability of cyclotomic equations by radicals via Gaussian periods and Lagrange resolvents

results.what: Proofs of the supplementary laws for −1 and ±2 (entry 56)
results.modern_name: First and second supplements to quadratic reciprocity
results.usually_credited_to: Stated by Fermat and Euler; proofs by Euler and Lagrange, and Gauss in the DA

results.what: Divisors of a²+b²+c²−ab−bc−ca coincide with those of a²+3b² (entry 57)
results.modern_name: Reduction of the ternary form to x²−xy+y², equivalent to x²+3y² for odd prime divisors (primes ≡1 mod 3)
q-continued fraction for a partial theta function (Eisenstein's continued fraction)
results.usually_credited_to: Eisenstein (1844, 'Transformations remarquables de quelques séries'); Gauss priority noted from the diary

deep.surprise_reason: This is a page of Gauss's famous mathematical diary (entries 51–58), published by Klein in 1903 and annotated many times since. The lemniscate start, the polygon supplement and the theta continued fraction (Eisenstein 1844) are all already credited to Gauss through it.

checkable.asserts: Primes ≥5 dividing a primitive value of x²−xy+y² are exactly those ≡1 mod 3 (same as for x²+3y²).

checkable.asserts: Euler's criterion (entry 52) for odd primes below 100.

transcription_corrections: Entry 56: the image reads 'demonstratae ut cetera' ('vt cetera'), not 'et cetera'. 'Ress.' abbreviates 'Residuis'. The struck word, transcribed 'pertro', is probably an aborted 'pertracta…'.
The marginal note reads 'Unde facile omnes series ubi exp[onentes] ser[iem] sec[undi] ordinis constituunt transformantur' ('exponents form a series of second order', i.e. quadratic exponents).
Line 1: the struck word is 'elasticam' and the superscript insertion is 'lemniscatam'. The transcription has this right; the closing parenthesis after the integral is in the original.
Entry 55: the superscript 'p' is inserted above 'unitate truncati' ('numeri primi p unitate truncati'), meaning the factors of p−1.
'commentus sum' and 'Jan. 12' belong to the ∫dx/ⁿ√(1−xⁿ) entry. The 'Methodus facilis' entry follows without its own date, and its integrand is x^(n−1)dx/(1+x^m).
